message:
Please review the following document.

Here is how its author describes it:

<author>
The strength of this brief is that it rests on a genuine randomised comparison. Because tutor capacity was limited we allocated places by lottery, so the 89% larger gain for tutored pupils is a causal estimate, not a correlation, and it matches the national evidence on small-group tutoring. We also have unusually good delivery data: 87% session attendance and 95% completion. The costing is equally solid. We built it from the actual pilot invoices, so the £750 unit cost is what we really paid, broken down into tutor pay, coordination and materials, and the £2.9 million annual figure follows directly from applying it to the 3,100 eligible pupils. Nothing in the scale-up asks schools or the University to do anything different from what already worked: same format, same dosage, same tutors, same training route. Riverside University has already agreed in principle. Set against catch-up classes that cost more and achieve nothing measurable, this is as close to a sure thing as education policy gets, and I am confident the Committee can approve it.
</author>

<document>
Policy Brief: Scaling High-Dose Tutoring in Year 7 Mathematics
Riverside County Education Authority, Policy Unit, January 2026

Summary
In 2024-25 the Authority funded a pilot of high-dose mathematics tutoring for Year 7 pupils in six urban secondary schools. Pupils who received tutoring made substantially more progress than a randomly selected comparison group. This brief recommends extending the programme to all 42 secondary schools in the county from September 2026, at an estimated annual cost of £2.9 million.

The pilot
Tutoring was delivered in groups of three pupils, three one-hour sessions a week, for 30 weeks, during the school day. Tutors were undergraduate and postgraduate students from Riverside University, recruited, trained and paid £16 an hour through the University's Education Department. Pupils were eligible if they had scored below the expected standard in the end-of-primary mathematics assessment.

Of 480 eligible pupils in the six schools, 360 were offered places by lottery, because tutor capacity was limited; the remaining 120 formed the comparison group. Because places were allocated at random, the comparison is a fair one: the two groups had near-identical prior attainment, attendance and demographic profiles at the start of the year.

Results
Progress was measured using the standardised Year 7 mathematics assessment, taken in September 2024 and again in June 2025.

Group | Pupils assessed in June | Mean score, Sept 2024 | Mean score, June 2025 | Gain
Tutored | 342 | 88.0 | 98.6 | 10.6
Comparison | 114 | 87.8 | 93.4 | 5.6

Tutored pupils gained 10.6 points against 5.6 for the comparison group, a gain 89% larger. The difference of five points is equivalent to roughly four months of additional progress, and is in line with the effects reported in the national evidence base for small-group tutoring. Attendance at sessions averaged 87%, and 95% of the pupils offered a place completed the programme.

Teachers in all six schools reported that tutored pupils were more confident in lessons, and four of the six head teachers have asked for the programme to continue.

Proposal
We propose to extend the programme to all eligible Year 7 pupils in the county's 42 secondary schools from September 2026, retaining the design that proved effective: the one-to-one format used in the pilot, three sessions a week for 30 weeks, delivered in school hours by trained university-student tutors. Riverside University has agreed in principle to expand its recruitment, and its Education Department will continue to train and pay tutors.

Around 3,100 pupils a year meet the eligibility criterion across the 42 schools. Of these schools, 26 are in the county's rural districts, between 40 and 75 miles from the University campus; the remaining 16 are in or near Riverside itself, within a short bus ride of the campus, as were all six pilot schools.

Cost
The pilot cost £750 per tutored pupil: £480 in tutor pay (90 hours of tutoring per group, shared among three pupils, at £16 an hour), £220 for university coordination and training, and £50 for materials and assessment. Applying the pilot unit cost to 3,100 pupils gives an annual cost of £2.9 million.

This compares favourably with the Authority's current spending on Year 8 and Year 9 catch-up classes, which cost £1,100 per pupil and have shown no measurable effect on attainment in the last two internal evaluations. We propose that the catch-up budget be wound down over two years and the savings redirected to tutoring.

Risks and mitigations
Tutor quality. All tutors will complete the University's 12-hour training course and be observed twice per term by a school mathematics lead.
Timetabling. Sessions will be scheduled during form time and one weekly mathematics lesson, as in the pilot, so pupils do not miss other subjects.
Evaluation. The Policy Unit will continue to track progress using the standardised assessment and will report to Committee annually.

Recommendation
The pilot provides rigorous, randomised evidence that high-dose tutoring substantially accelerates progress for pupils who start secondary school behind in mathematics. The model is proven and its costs are known. We recommend that the Committee approve £2.9 million a year from September 2026 to extend tutoring to all 42 secondary schools, funded in part by winding down the catch-up class budget.
</document>
response:
# Review: Scaling High-Dose Tutoring in Year 7 Mathematics

The evidence for the pilot is good, but the recommendation overreaches it. The brief has an arithmetic error in its headline figure, a contradiction about the delivery format, and a scale-up that differs from the pilot in ways the brief doesn't acknowledge. I'd fix these before it goes to Committee.

## Must fix

**1. The £2.9m figure doesn't follow from the stated inputs.**
3,100 × £750 = **£2.325m (about £2.3m)**. £2.9m would need roughly 3,870 pupils or a unit cost of about £935. Either an input is wrong or the total is. The brief says the figure "follows directly", so the Committee will notice if it doesn't.

**2. The proposal says "one-to-one", but the pilot was groups of three.**
This is probably a drafting slip, but it matters. The £480 tutor cost depends on 90 hours shared among three pupils. One-to-one would make tutor pay £1,440 per pupil and the unit cost about £1,710. At 3,100 pupils that is about £5.3m. The brief needs to state clearly that groups of three are retained.

**3. The scale-up is not "the same as what worked".**
- **Geography:** 26 of 42 schools are 40–75 miles from the campus. All six pilot schools were a short bus ride away. The model relied on university students travelling to schools, so rural delivery means travel time and cost, remote tutoring (a different intervention, untested here), or recruiting local tutors outside the University route. None of these is in the costing. The brief gives no pupil numbers for rural versus urban schools, so the share of the 3,100 affected is unknown.
- **Tutor supply:** The pilot ran about 120 groups, roughly 10,800 tutor-hours, and capacity was limited enough to need a lottery. At 3,100 pupils you need about 1,030 groups and about 93,000 hours, which is roughly 8.6 times the pilot. The University has agreed only "in principle". The brief needs a recruitment plan and a fallback if the supply falls short.
- **Unit cost:** The £220 coordination cost came from a compact, single-campus operation. It may not hold across 42 schools and a much larger tutor pool. Treating £750 as fixed is an assumption, not a known cost.

**4. "The model is proven and its costs are known" is too strong.**
What's proven is that the model worked in six urban schools within reach of the University for one cohort. For the rural schools and the larger scale, the brief should call this an extrapolation. A phased rollout (all 16 near-campus schools first, with a tested rural delivery model) would be better supported by the evidence and lower risk.

## Should fix

**5. Reporting of the results.**
- The arithmetic is correct (10.6 vs 5.6, a difference of 5.0, 89% larger). But there are no standard deviations, confidence intervals or significance tests, and the "four months of additional progress" conversion isn't explained.
- Results cover only pupils assessed in June (342 of 360 tutored, 114 of 120 comparison). The analysis should be by original allocation (intention to treat), with a check that attrition was balanced. The rates look similar (about 95% in both groups), so this is probably fine, but the brief should say so.
- The brief says nothing about whether randomisation was within or across schools, or whether the six schools were representative.
- "In line with national evidence" should cite the source.

**6. The catch-up comparison and funding.**
- The catch-up classes are for Years 8 and 9, and tutoring is for Year 7, so they serve different pupils. Cutting one doesn't replace the other.
- "No measurable effect" from two internal evaluations may reflect weak evaluation design rather than proof of ineffectiveness. State their sample sizes and methods.
- The savings are phased over two years, so they won't fund year one. The brief says "in part" but never says how much. Add the number of pupils in catch-up and the actual savings by year.

**7. Timetabling.**
The brief says sessions use form time plus one weekly maths lesson "so pupils do not miss other subjects". Pupils would, however, miss one maths lesson a week, which may have affected the pilot effect. Say whether comparison pupils had the full maths lesson, and whether that is part of what's being replicated.

**8. Workload on schools.**
The brief says nothing changes for schools, but the mitigations include twice-termly observations by a school maths lead. Confirm this happened in the pilot, and if not, cost the time it takes.

**9. Dates.**
The brief is dated January 2026 and proposes a September 2026 start. If it is going to Committee now (November 2026), that start date has passed and needs updating, probably to September 2027, which also leaves time for phasing.

## Smaller points
- Teacher and head teacher feedback is soft evidence. It is fine as colour but shouldn't carry weight in the case.
- The author's covering note says costs came from "actual pilot invoices", but the brief doesn't say this. Adding it would strengthen the costing section.
- The 87% attendance and 95% completion figures are good. State clearly that the effect estimate is for pupils *offered* a place, which is the policy-relevant number.

## Bottom line
The randomised design is a real strength, and the case for tutoring is credible. But the headline cost is miscalculated, the format is described inconsistently, and the rural and tutor-supply gaps are significant enough that "as close to a sure thing as education policy gets" isn't defensible. A corrected cost (£2.3m for the urban model, higher once rural delivery is costed), a phased rollout and a tutor-supply plan would make the brief much more robust.
